nameStory: The "large lace-border" gets its charming name from the delicate, lacy pattern that decorates the edges of its wings, resembling fine lacework trim on a Victorian dress. Among the lace-border moths, this species earned the "large" designation because of its impressive wingspan that can stretch over an inch across. The intricate border pattern looks almost like it was hand-stitched by a master craftsperson.
description: The Large Lace-border Moth is a delicate member of the geometer moth family, known for their slender bodies and broad, graceful wings. These moths have a wingspan of about 1 to 1.2 inches, making them noticeably larger than many of their relatives. Their wings display intricate lacy patterns along the borders that give them their distinctive name. Like other geometer moths, their caterpillars are the famous "inchworms" that loop along as they crawl.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic lacy, intricate pattern along the wing borders that resembles delicate embroidered trim - this lacework is more elaborate than similar small moths

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Wingspan measures about 1 to 1.2 inches across when fully spread - noticeably larger than most other small white or pale moths you'll encounter

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender, delicate body typical of geometer moths - feels almost fragile if you gently handle one, much thinner than chunky sphinx moths or robust underwing moths

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings horizontally outspread rather than folded tent-like over the body, creating a distinctive flat, spread-eagle silhouette

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat weak, fluttery motion rather than strong, direct flight - often seems to drift or flutter around lights

habitat: Large Lace-border Moths can be found throughout New England's diverse habitats, from suburban gardens to wild meadows and forest edges. They're particularly drawn to areas with their host plants like apple trees, blueberry bushes, clover patches, and dandelions, making them common in orchards, old fields, and even well-planted backyards. Look for them around outdoor lights in areas near flowering plants and fruit trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, so you might spot the first individuals of the year during warm late spring evenings around outdoor lights.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through summer months - this is the best time to find adults flying around lights or resting on vegetation during the day. Caterpillars are actively feeding on host plants.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue flying into early September, though numbers decline as the season progresses. Late-season individuals may look somewhat worn with faded wing patterns.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - the species overwinters in a dormant stage, likely as pupae in the soil or leaf litter.

funFact: The caterpillars of Large Lace-border Moths are incredibly versatile eaters, munching on everything from apple trees to dandelions to blueberry bushes - they're like the ultimate garden buffet diners, equally happy with your prized fruit trees or the "weeds" you're trying to get rid of!
confusionNotes: Large Lace-border Moths can be confused with other small, pale geometer moths, but their size is a key distinguisher - if the wingspan is over an inch with intricate lacy wing borders, you're likely looking at a Large Lace-border rather than its smaller cousins.
contextualKnowledge: The name "geometer" means "earth measurer" and refers to how the caterpillars seem to measure the ground as they move in their characteristic inching motion, arching their backs with each step like tiny living rulers.
compareHints: Since this is the only Scopula species recorded in our New England dataset, compare it with other geometer moths in the region. Large Lace-border Moths are distinguished by their relatively large size (1+ inch wingspan) and elaborate lacy wing patterns, whereas most other small geometers are either smaller, plainer, or have different pattern types like waves or spots rather than intricate lacework. The combination of size and delicate border patterning makes this species fairly distinctive among New England's geometer moth community.
